#9298. How a Freak Flood Revealed the Gut-Brain Axis

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

“There is a tide in the affairs of men, which taken at the flood, leads on to fortune.” —William Shakespeare

In May 2000, the Canadian town of Walkerton was flooded after a heavy rain. The town’s water supply became contaminated with E. coli and Campylobacter jejuni. It was caused by overflow from a cow and chicken farm known to have problems containing their pathogens. Over two thousand of the five thousand townsfolk became seriously ill. Seven died. The town basically shut down. And then it was noticed that hundreds of these people, after recovering from their original infections, came down with IBS. They also became depressed.

Although E. coli was present in the water, C. jejuni arguably played a bigger role in the disaster. C. jejuni is sensitive to stomach acids, which quickly killed many of the microbes. But people who regularly took antacids had lower levels of acidity, allowing more of the C. jejuni to pass through. Those using proton-pump inhibitors were twice as likely to get sick from C. jejuni.

Although diminished, many of these pathogens still made it to the intestines. These bacteria were recently inside a cow or a chicken, so they were pretty much at home in the human gut. In cows and chickens, C. jejuni is a commensal. Why it goes berserk in a human gut is unclear, but C. jejuni is potent: It is the number-one cause of diarrhea in the United States, ahead of Salmonella and E. coli. The odds are good that you’ve had it at least once in your life.

In response to C. jejuni, special cells lining the intestines secreted serotonin, which increased peristalsis in anticipation of purging.

C. jejuni caused anxiety even without a full-blown infection. Cells lining the gut called neuropods detected the invasion, causing the nervous system to go on alert before the immune system kicked in. This was an early shot across the bow; the brain now knew something was up down below.

Some heroic microbes emerged to face down the C. jejuni, including Bifidobacteria and Lactobacillus species. They worked to outcompete and crowd out the C. jejuni, preventing them from sticking to the cells lining the gut. Ironically, those who had taken antibiotics recently had lost this microbial defense and they were hit harder by the C. jejuni.

Sadly, the city officials of Walkerton insisted that the water was safe, and people kept drinking it. The C. jejuni soon overwhelmed their microbial defenses, eating through the mucus lining the gut and leaving tender gut cells exposed to infection.

Once attached to a cell, C. jejuni makes a toxin that stops gut cells from dividing. Without division, gut cells can't renew themselves and when they die, the gut lining begins to leak. A leaky gut leads to inflammation. Sure enough, the citizens of Walkerton came down with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), along with its accompanying depression and anxiety.

Stephen Collins, a professor at McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario, took the two-hour drive to Walkerton to see if there was a way to snatch some useful research from the town's misery.

For eight years Collins followed this group of unlucky Canadians and found that many of them had suffered intractable IBS ever since their initial infection. Collins recognized this as post-infectious IBS, which was first seen in soldiers who had picked up dysentery during World War II. About one in eight cases of IBS starts this way. Collins discovered a significant association between IBS and the mental conditions of depression and anxiety.

Intriguingly, Collins found that people with pre-existing depression had double the risk of contracting IBS. This observation underlines the dual nature of the gut-brain dialogue. It creates a positive-feedback loop, a vicious cycle that can be hard to break.

The initial infection caused the immune system to move swiftly to eradicate the offending bacteria. But in some people, the immune response failed to wind down after eliminating the pathogens, leading to treatment-resistant IBS.

Collins was joined in the research project by Premysl Bercik, also of McMaster University. Bercik took fecal matter from IBS patients and transplanted it into mice. The mice subsequently developed anxiety-like behavior, demonstrating that gut microbiota can affect mental states and that, intriguingly, those states can be transferred from one animal to another. The idea that mental states could be transmitted via fecal transplant took most scientists by surprise.

In the wake of the disaster, Walkerton erected a waterfall commemorating the victims. But the people who got IBS and became depressed started an important conversation about how the gut is related to the brain. Today, their suffering is also memorialized by the astonishing revelations of the gut-brain axis.

John K. Marshall et al., “Eight Year Prognosis of Postinfectious Irritable Bowel Syndrome Following Waterborne Bacterial Dysentery,” Gut 59, no. 5 (May 1, 2010): 605–11, doi:10.1136/gut.2009.202234.

Wei, Li, Lasantha Ratnayake, Gabby Phillips, Chris C. McGuigan, Steve V. Morant, Robert W. Flynn, Isla S. Mackenzie, and Thomas M. MacDonald. “Acid Suppression Medications and Bacterial Gastroenteritis: A Population-Based Cohort Study.” British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology, January 1, 2016, n/a-n/a. doi:10.1111/bcp.13205.

Altekruse, S. F., N. J. Stern, P. I. Fields, and D. L. Swerdlow. “Campylobacter C. jejuni--an Emerging Foodborne Pathogen.” Emerging Infectious Diseases 5, no. 1 (1999): 28–35.

In 1824, studying a set of large fossil bones discovered in a quarry near Oxford two centuries earlier, the English theologian, geologist, and paleontologist William Buckland kept looking at the fragment of the lower jaw. Something didn’t add up. As he examined it more closely, he realized these were not the remains of an elephant, as previously thought, but of an enormous carnivorous reptile with no analogue in the fossil record or in the living world.

He christened it Megalosaurus — the first named dinosaur — and set out to compose a complete account of the ancient beast.

Because nobody knew what dinosaurs looked like, he needed an exceptional scientific illustrator whose unbridled imagination and disciplined draughtsmanship could enflesh the bones of the mysterious creature. Taken by a particularly excellent drawing of the jaw of an extinct hyena, he obtained a letter of introduction to the artist, tucked it into his coat pocket, and boarded a coach across Devonshire, hoping to be received.

William took one book to accompany him on the long ride — a weighty new volume by paleontology founding father Georges Couvier, summarizing his pioneering research on the fossil bones of quadrupeds. With gaping disbelief, he watched another passenger take out that same book and begin paging through it. The conversation was inevitable and the realization quick: She was the artist he was traveling to meet. Cuvier himself had sent her the book in gratitude for her contribution.

Perhaps because she had lost her mother while still an infant, Mary Morland had grown up fascinated by deep time, by the slow-burning beauty of minerals, by the way fossils immortalized the ephemerality of the flesh. After devouring Couvier’s books as a teenager, she taught herself draughtsmanship and unlearned what her culture had told her she could be: Determined to become an artist of science, she sent her specimen illustrations to Couvier himself.

The venerable scientist was so taken with the young woman’s work that he published it alongside his studies. Word spread across the scientific community and soon she was illustrating other books and modeling rare specimens in leather.

Unlike most women of her time, whose standard path to subsistence was marriage, Mary could now make a living by her own work. If she married, it would only be for love. Her love was the science of time: She kept drawing paleontological specimens, grew an impressive mineral collection, became a fossil geologist herself.

By the time she met William that day on the coach, she was an old maid in her late twenties and one of the era’s most esteemed scientific illustrators. They started on the dinosaur work immediately.

Within a year, Mary Morland was Mary Buckland. Their home became a miniature Alexandria of science books, light pouring in from candle-holders made of ichthyosaurus vertebrae, fossils lining every sideboard. Their dining room housed a menagerie of frogs and snakes. Guinea pigs ran regularly across the table. A pony occasionally rode past, a laughing child on its back.

One of their surviving children would later recount that Mary not only illustrated William’s studies but, with her “great mental powers, habits of perseverance and order, tempered by excellent judgment,” she “gave to them a polish which added not a little to their merit.”

Despite their fourteen-year age difference, she outlived him by just over a year, channeling her bereavement in studying marine bryozoans — coral-like saltwater creatures — with her daughter. Hours before her death, Mary was still bent over her microscope, entranced by a new specimen.

Mary and William were buried alongside one another, their entwined fossils to be discovered by some paleontologist of the far future: What is love if not the mutual belonging of our passions and our bones.

#9296. New book explores how Ukraine’s artists are shaping the memory of war

Cover illustration by Kyiv-based Ukrainian artist Sergiy Maidukov

As the war grinds on in Ukraine, almost five years after Russia’s full-scale invasion, The Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins reminds us in her timely and sobering new book how artists and writers register the human cost of the conflict.

“The argument of this book is that the literature and art made by these people, some of whom have lost their lives, will shape the war’s memory,” Higgins boldly asserts. Artists, writers, poets and filmmakers are her vital and sympathetic touchstones across cities such as Kyiv, Kharkiv and Lviv.

“When a friend, the defence and security editor of The Guardian, suggested I might think about going to Ukraine, I agreed immediately that it was a good idea,” she writes. “I said it lightly, impulsively, and without realising that going there would change me.”

This odyssey begins in the autumn of 2022, encompassing three years of reporting trips to Ukraine. The arc of the narrative is epic and emotional, from arriving in Kyiv on a bright, beautiful day (10 October) to a final documentary account of the destruction of Bakhmut in the east, where an elderly lady called Nina surveys streets blitzed by shell holes that “were once perfectly ordinary”.

Along the way, Higgins deftly interweaves personal milestones such as slowly grasping the Ukrainian language—who knew “verbs of motion” could be so onerous?—detailing how “the war leaked into every [language] lesson”. Dealing with the anger felt by Ukrainians facing “the outrage of violence” is another test for the author, who anchors her account by observing the impact of Ukrainian art and artists, both historic and contemporary.

As testament to the violence and destruction, Higgins draws on a film by the Kharkiv artists Daniil Revkovskyi and Andrii Rachynskyi shown in the Ukrainian pavilion at the 2024 Venice Biennale. Civilians. Invasion (2023) is an hour-long collage of unedited videos found online that mirror the true reality of constant bombs and bullets.

Higgins’s survey of artists is essential as a journal of record, bringing to the fore figures such as Marharyta Polovinko, whose macabre, penetrating drawings of roaming monsters can be set, Higgins argues, alongside the work of Spanish artist Francisco Goya—famed for The Disasters of War (1810-20)—or the First World War and Weimar imagery of the German painter Otto Dix. Immortalising these creative figures, who may go unnoticed outside Ukraine, is a significant commemorative act (Polovinko was killed in action in 2025, aged 31).

A trained classicist, Higgins frames the events and trauma of the war through Greek mythology. She likens the character of Cassandra—who was condemned to prophesy only the truth but never be believed—to “resolute Ukrainian women, eloquent and truth-telling”, neatly segueing into one of Ukraine’s greatest works of literature, a seminal poem written by Lesya Ukrainka around 1907 (Cassandra: A Dramatic Poem).

Victoria Amelina, a Ukrainian novelist and war crimes investigator who died aged 37 in July 2023 from severe injuries sustained during a Russian missile strike, is one of these “Pale Cassandras”. Amelina was instrumental in bringing to light the buried journal of the late writer Volodymyr Vakulenko who documented life under occupation.

In commemorating friends and colleagues like Amelina, Higgins is searing and eloquent. “[…] grief leaked out of me,” she says, “and I felt like a vessel with no shape, porous, lacking capacity to hold anything.” Such frank admissions could jar but in shaping a war’s memory, this narrative benefits from such measured, personal interludes.

Cultural erasure is a weapon of war: at least 120 Ukrainian museums have been damaged in the conflict, according to the country’s culture ministry. Russian president Vladimir Putin is not only attempting to annihilate the military and political leadership, but also its cultural warriors in a ruthless bid to vanquish the existence of a sovereign Ukraine. Higgins’s book is a bulwark against this campaign; as a personal memoir it is deeply affecting, and as a journalistic record it is transformative.

• Ukrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War, by Charlotte Higgins, published by Jonathan Cape, 272pp, £22 (hb), 20 August

“Rule of Two Walls”, showing at the Tribeca Film Festival, follows artists in Ukraine after the launch of Russia’s invasion

The guidelines aim to make international laws readily accessible to soldiers on the ground, and reflects Ukraine's experience in the war against Russia

President Zelensky's wife gave a video address to visitors of the show in Venice

The video and installation artist donated her prize money to the Ukrainian armed forces

“If you can fall in love again and again,” Henry Miller wrote as he contemplated the measure of a life well lived on the precipice of turning eighty, “if you can forgive as well as forget, if you can keep from growing sour, surly, bitter and cynical… you’ve got it half licked.”

Seven years earlier, the great British philosopher, mathematician, historian, and Nobel laureate Bertrand Russell (May 18, 1872–February 2, 1970) considered the same abiding question at the same life-stage in a wonderful short essay titled “How to Grow Old,” penned in his eighty-first year and later published in Portraits from Memory and Other Essays (public library).

Russell places at the heart of a fulfilling life the dissolution of the personal ego into something larger. Drawing on the longstanding allure of rivers as existential metaphors, he writes:

Make your interests gradually wider and more impersonal, until bit by bit the walls of the ego recede, and your life becomes increasingly merged in the universal life. An individual human existence should be like a river — small at first, narrowly contained within its banks, and rushing passionately past rocks and over waterfalls. Gradually the river grows wider, the banks recede, the waters flow more quietly, and in the end, without any visible break, they become merged in the sea, and painlessly lose their individual being.

In a sentiment which philosopher and comedian Emily Levine would echo in her stirring reflection on facing her own death with equanimity, Russell builds on the legacy of Darwin and Freud, who jointly established death as an organizing principle of modern life, and concludes:

The man who, in old age, can see his life in this way, will not suffer from the fear of death, since the things he cares for will continue. And if, with the decay of vitality, weariness increases, the thought of rest will not be unwelcome. I should wish to die while still at work, knowing that others will carry on what I can no longer do and content in the thought that what was possible has been done.

Portraits from Memory and Other Essays is an uncommonly potent packet of wisdom in its totality. Complement this particular fragment with Nobel laureate André Gide on how happiness increases with age, Ursula K. Le Guin on aging and what beauty really means, and Grace Paley on the art of growing older — the loveliest thing I’ve ever read on the subject — then revisit Russell on critical thinking, power-knowledge vs. love-knowledge, what “the good life” really means, why “fruitful monotony” is essential for happiness, and his remarkable response to a fascist’s provocation.

#9294. Advanced Tree Counting: Mathematical Layouts With `sibling-index()` And `sibling-count()`

Durgesh Rajubhai Pawar is a freelance developer dedicated to building high-performance, accessible web applications. He specializes in orchestrating complex … More about Durgesh ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

You know that thing where you have a grid of cards, and you want them to fade in one after another? That staggered cascade effect. Looks great. Should be simple. And yet every time I’ve built it, the implementation has made me feel like I’m doing something fundamentally stupid.

See the Pen [Dynamic Staggered Animations with CSS sibling-index() [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/zxowBog) by Durgesh.

Because the options were always the same. Say you want staggered animation delays on a list of 10 items. You either wrote a Sass loop that spat out a dozen :nth-child() rules, each one hardcoding a --index variable for that specific position:

Ten items. Ten rules. If the list grows to 50? You cap it and hope for the best, or set up a Sass loop that generates hundreds of selectors at build time. Engineers like Roman Komarov have come up with O(âˆšN) strategies — legitimately clever stuff — but you still end up with 63 rules to cover 1,023 elements.

Or you looped through elements in JavaScript and set inline styles. style="--index: 3". Right there in the DOM. Works fine. Also spreads layout concerns across your scripts and quietly breaks six months later when someone refactors the component without realizing the CSS depends on a JavaScript-injected variable.

Both approaches have always bugged me for the same reason: you’re telling the browser something it already knows. The browser built the DOM tree. It knows which element is the third child. It has the data. CSS just couldn’t access it.

One line. Works for 5 items or 5,000. No event listeners. No mutation observers. No re-renders.

sibling-index() and sibling-count() are part of the CSS Values and Units Module Level 5 spec (Section 9, if you’re the type who reads W3C drafts for fun). The proposal was approved via CSSWG issue #4559 after substantial discussion. The functions themselves take no arguments — you just use them.

Both functions resolve to — not , an actual number. That means you can throw them into calc(), min(), max(), round(), mod(), trigonometric stuff like sin() and cos(). When you write calc(sibling-index() * 100ms), CSS handles the type coercion and spits out a valid value. No tricks needed. Compare that with counter(), which returns a string and can only live inside content on pseudo-elements — it’s a different thing entirely.

One clarification that trips people up: :nth-child() is a selector. It picks elements. It doesn’t produce a value. You can’t write calc(:nth-child() * 10px) — that’s not valid CSS. sibling-index() does the opposite. It sits inside your declarations and gives you a number you can calculate with. They solve different problems, and until now we’ve been duct-taping :nth-child() into a role it was never designed for.

Once it clicks that these are just integers, ideas come fast.

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

Want the last item to animate first? Subtract:

Last child gets (N - N) * 80ms = 0ms — it fires instantly. First child gets (N - 1) * 80ms. The animation kicks off the moment the page loads instead of pausing for an awkward beat.

Stop counting children manually to set percentages:

Five tabs? 20% each. Add a sixth? 16.66%. Remove two? 25%. No media queries, no resize observers, no JavaScript at all.

That said, you can imagine a scenario where too many items make for really narrow tabs, at which point you might want to go with something else, perhaps a Flexbox wrapping solution.

Spread colors evenly across the color wheel:

Three items get hues 120Â° apart. Twelve items get 30Â° increments. The palette adapts to whatever’s in the DOM, which is the kind of thing you’d normally reach for a JavaScript color library to do.

Distributing items in a circle used to mean calculating sine and cosine in JavaScript. CSS now has sin() and cos() natively (Juan Diego RodrÃ­guez has a great practical walkthrough of these on CSS-Tricks), and combined with tree-counting, the whole thing collapses into pure CSS:

Six items? Hexagon. Eight? Octagon. Add or remove items, and the layout recalculates. No JavaScript computing coordinates.

First card stacks highest, last card gets 0. Flip the math if you want the reverse.

These are worth going through individually because they’re not obvious from the spec.

sibling-index() and sibling-count() operate on the DOM tree, not the flattened visual tree. This distinction will absolutely bite you with Web Components.

Say you have a custom element with this shadow DOM:

If you style .internal with sibling-index(), it returns 2. Always. Even if the projects 300 elements. The function sees two children of

in the shadow tree — the and the .internal div. Projected light DOM content doesn’t exist as far as the count is concerned.

There’s also a security thing going on here. If a light DOM stylesheet tries to reach into a component via ::part() and use sibling-index(), the browser returns 0. Flat zero. It’s a deliberate wall to prevent external CSS from probing the internal structure of third-party components. Honestly, I think that’s the right call.

::before and ::after aren’t siblings. They don’t show up in sibling-count() and they don’t have their own sibling-index(). But — and this is the part that’ll save you a debugging session — you can use these functions inside pseudo-element declarations. When you write #target::before { width: calc(sibling-index() * 10px); }, it evaluates sibling-index() against #target, not against the pseudo-element. The pseudo-element isn’t a real node, so the function traces back to its originating element. Same story with ::slotted(*)::before — it checks the slotted element’s index in the light DOM.

This one burned me. Elements with display: none vanish from the layout tree. They take up no space. Screen readers don’t see them. But they’re still in the DOM.

Since sibling-index() reads the DOM tree, not the layout tree, hidden elements get counted:

Cherry is 3, not 2. The hidden banana still holds its spot.

This doesn’t matter for most layouts. But if you’re building something like a search filter that hides non-matching items with display: none, your staggered animations and circular layouts will develop gaps. The visible items keep their original, non-sequential indexes. For anything that depends on continuous counting — radial menus, proportional widths — you’ll need to actually remove filtered nodes from the DOM instead of just hiding them. Or fall back to JavaScript-managed indexes.

Note: visibility: hidden and opacity: 0 count too, but that feels more intuitive since those elements still take up space. display: none is the sneaky one because the element disappears visually but still occupies a DOM slot.

This is subtle. If you try to centralize the index on a parent:

…that --idx resolves right there on .parent. It grabs the parent’s own sibling index, locks it to that number, and every child inherits that single fixed value. Every child gets the same number. Almost certainly not what you want or expect.

The fix is simple — put the function on the elements that need it:

The CSSWG has discussed an inherits: declaration addition to @property that could theoretically fix this. If you haven’t used @property, it lets you define a custom property’s type, initial value, and inheritance behavior — way more control than a raw --variable. But the inherits: declaration idea is still in early CSSWG discussion, not baked into any spec draft. It could be years before it lands — or it might not land at all. Even with @property today, there’s no mechanism to say “don’t evaluate yet, wait for the child.” So for now, just apply directly.

Changing the DOM — i.e., adding, removing, reordering children — triggers style recalculation for affected siblings. The browser handles this during the cascade phase (before layout and paint), so it’s faster than the old approach of looping in JavaScript and stamping inline styles.

But there’s a real cost if you push it. Inserting an element at the beginning of a container with 10,000 children forces the engine to recalculate the sibling index for all 10,000 elements after it. For normal stuff — navigation, card grids, tab bars — you’ll never notice. For a live stock ticker or an infinite-scroll feed with thousands of nodes constantly churning, keep using JavaScript-managed indexes inside your virtualization window. These functions are fast. They’re not zero-cost.

As of writing, Chrome/Edge 138 shipped these functions in stable releases (June 2025), and Safari 26.2 followed. Firefox hasn’t shipped them in stable yet, but Mozilla’s spec position is positive and implementation work is actively underway — tracked under Bugzilla issue #1953973. Check caniuse for the latest before you ship.

Chrome and Safari together cover roughly 75–80% of global traffic. That’s a strong majority, but Firefox’s absence means you still need a fallback.

For shipping today, @supports is your friend:

Static fallback for Firefox. Mathematical layout for everyone else. Nobody gets a broken page.

This needs saying because it’s easy to get excited and forget: these functions are purely visual. They change how things look. They don’t change what things mean.

If you use sibling-index() math to visually reorder a list — via order or grid placement — a screen reader still reads the DOM in source order. Keyboard tab order follows the DOM, too. Visual layout and semantic structure will contradict each other, and that’s an accessibility failure.

For interactive components like data grids, radial menus, or custom listboxes that lean on tree-counting for layout, you still need JavaScript to sync ARIA attributes. aria-posinset and aria-setsize have no idea what CSS is calculating. If your CSS says “this is visually item 3 of 7” but ARIA says something different (or nothing), assistive technology users get a broken experience.

On the debugging side, recent versions of Chrome DevTools let you inspect computed sibling-index() and sibling-count() values directly in the Elements panel, which helps when the math isn’t doing what you expect.

The current spec only counts all element siblings. But the CSSWG has documented a planned extension in issue #9572: an of argument, matching what :nth-child() already supports.

Something like sibling-index(of .active) would let you count only siblings matching a specific selector. An element that’s the eighth child overall but the third .active child would return 3. For dynamic UIs where you’re filtering or toggling visibility, that would keep the index sequential without requiring DOM manipulation.

There’s also been CSSWG discussion around children-count() and descendant-count() functions — the first would tell you how many children an element has (useful for parent-driven layouts), the second would count all descendants recursively. Both are still at the proposal stage, but they’d round out the tree-counting story: sibling-index() and sibling-count() give you the horizontal view (where am I among my peers?), while children-count() and descendant-count() would give you the vertical view (what’s below me?).

That feeling I mentioned at the top — writing ten :nth-child() rules for a staggered animation and wondering if you’re missing something obvious? You weren’t. The obvious thing just didn’t exist yet.

#9293. How Emotions Shape Our Impressions of Others

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

This post was co-authored with Rebecca Schlegel, Professor of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Texas A&M University.

What do you think of when you hear the word stereotype? This term has become highly polarizing in today’s society. It probably brings to mind ideas like social justice; diversity, equity, and inclusion training; meritocracy; oppression; wokeness; and equity. You probably have emotions about these ideas, possibly strong ones, and have attitudes about what we should do as a society about these things. But what comes to mind is probably not what psychologists mean when they study stereotypes, and people are often surprised by the role of emotions in shaping what we think about others.

When viewed through a psychological lens, stereotypes are not good or bad. They are byproducts of how people think. The human mind operates by creating categories or “bins” and using those bins to collect related information. As children learn language, for example, they might create a bin called “dogs,” and place everything that is four-legged and furry into that bin. This leads to some common errors, such as children calling a cat a “dog” because it is four-legged and furry. Typically, these errors are corrected by others (a parent explains it is not a dog, but a cat), and the categories get adjusted as children learn what information goes in what bin. This structure is critical for functioning in the world—we can enter a new situation and know what to expect because we’ve been in similar situations before. Without the category of “dog,” we would have to treat every encounter with a dog as a new experience. With the category of “dog,” we have some idea of how the animal will behave and what we should and shouldn’t do when encountering a dog, and we can talk with other people about our experiences with dogs to share information. Overall, categories help us learn faster and function better.

We use this same categorization process to make sense of the many different types of people we encounter in the world. From an early age, we learn categories and place people into those categories. We learn some bins at very young ages, such as family versus stranger. As we grow and learn, the categories are adjusted based on correcting errors and greater experience. Placing people into those categories allows us to quickly respond—children learn to treat someone in the bin of “stranger” very differently than they treat someone in the bin of “family.”

Stereotypes refer to the information and beliefs we put in the bins we have learned for groups of people. Just as people might associate the bin of “dog” with concepts like loyal or energetic, people associate bins for groups of people with different concepts. For example, people may associate the category of “football player” with concepts like “strong.” At their root, stereotypes are mental shortcuts that people use to make sense of other people just as they do with other types of categories in the world. Creating the bins and putting information in the bins is just a feature of how our brain makes sense of a complicated world.

The challenge comes when we develop emotions about the bins we use. One person might associate the bin of “dog” with loyalty and develop good feelings about dogs, whereas another person might associate the bin of “dog” with aggression and develop negative feelings about them. In the same way, people attach good or bad feelings to bins for categories of people. This process—where an emotion is attached to a category or idea—is called attitude formation. The bin is no longer neutral—there is an emotional tag that changes how you interact with the members of that category. If the bin of “dogs” is attached to negative feelings or fear, you avoid dogs. Similarly, you are disposed to act differently toward categories of people associated with negative emotions versus groups you associate with positive emotions. These emotions can be powerful guides to behavior.

The beliefs we hold about groups of people and the emotional responses we have toward the groups are different concepts in psychology. In daily life, however, these things often go hand in hand and are influenced by the messages we receive about groups. Societal views of smoking and smokers in the United States are an excellent example of how stereotypes (and the emotions they evoke) develop and can shift. From the 1920s through the 1960s, smoking was associated with glamor and wealth. This was the result of marketing by companies and striking images of celebrities in movies, ads, and television. Smoking was not only socially acceptable; it was a good thing—part of being a productive and engaged member of society. The group “smokers” had become associated with positive beliefs and positive emotions.

As the health consequences of smoking behavior and the resulting economic impact became clear, government officials took steps to change public perceptions of smoking. They banned cigarette advertisements, promoted anti-smoking campaigns, and prohibited companies from using terms that suggested particular brands were safer or healthy. Many of the campaigns were graphic and evoked strong emotion, such as images of smokers with cigarette burns in their clothes and yellowed teeth, diseased lungs, or people in wheelchairs struggling to breathe. These messages were not just providing information to people about the health risks—they were actively attempting to shift the stereotypes of smoking and smokers. Over time, “smokers” became associated with negative emotions and beliefs, and were viewed as dangerous, irresponsible, selfish, unhealthy, and disgusting. They were banned from restaurants, airplanes, workplaces, campuses, and stores.

In current society, there is a high level of concern and attitudes about stereotypes and what we should do about them. Stereotypes have become a focus of political debate and calls to action. However, from a psychological perspective, stereotypes exist because they are a byproduct of how people learn, think, and navigate a complex social world, and they cannot be removed. But we can understand how messages through advertising, media, and other sources affect the impressions we form about other people. Understanding how our impressions are formed can help all of us make more intentional evaluations about other people based on our own experiences and our personal values.

#9292. Polyvagal Theory and the Neurobiology of Connection: The Science of Rupture, Repair, and Reciprocity

“A purely disembodied human emotion is a nonentity,” William James wrote in his pioneering 1884 theory of how our bodies affect our feelings — the first great gauntlet thrown at the Cartesian dualism of body versus mind. In the century and a half since, we have come to see how the body and the mind converge in the healing of trauma; we have come to see consciousness itself as a full-body phenomenon.

Beyond the brain, no portion of the body shapes our mental and emotional landscape more profoundly than the tenth cranial nerve — the longest nerve of the autonomic nervous system that unconsciously governs the inner workings of the body. Known as the vagus nerve — from the Latin for “wandering,” a root shared with vagabond and vague — it meanders from the brain to the gut, touching every organ along the way with its tendrils, controlling everything from our heart rate and digestion to our reflexes and moods.

In James’s lifetime, it was believed that synaptic communication within the brain was electrical. But when neuroscience founding father Santiago Ramón y Cajal discovered a gap between neurons — a miniature abyss electricity could not cross — it became clear that something else must be transmitting the signals between neurons. In 1921, the German pharmacologist Otto Loewi confirmed the existence of these theorized chemical messengers by stimulating the vagus nerve of a frog and discovering in the secreted substance the first known neurotransmitter. Every thought, feeling, and mood that has ever swept across the sky of your mind was forecast by your neurotransmitters and executed by your vagus nerve.

A century after James, while working with premature babies, the psychiatrist Stephen Porges uncovered two distinct vagal pathways in the nervous system — the much older dorsal vagus, which evolved around 500 million years ago in a fish now extinct to regulate fear response and activate shutdown, and the ventral vagus, a uniquely mammalian development about 200 million old, controlling our capacity for connection and communication. This research became the foundation of polyvagal theory — the science of how the interplay of these two systems shapes our sense of safety and danger, shapes our attachment styles and relationship patterns, shapes our very ability to tolerate the risks of living necessary for being in love with life.

In the decades since, no one has championed polyvagal theory more ardently than the clinical psychologist Deb Dana. In her book The Polyvagal Theory in Therapy: Engaging the Rhythm of Regulation (public library), written for therapists, she explores how trauma automates our adaptive responses in a survival story that puts the fear-based dorsal vagus in command to induce collapse and dissociation, and how we can rewire our neural pathways toward the emotional safety of the ventral vagal state, where our capacity for curiosity, connection, and change flourishes.

Connectedness is a biological imperative, and at the top of the autonomic hierarchy is the ventral vagal pathway that supports feelings of safety and connection. The ventral vagus (sometimes called the “smart vagus” or “social vagus”) provides the neurobiological foundation for health, growth, and restoration. When the ventral vagus is active, our attention is toward connection. We seek opportunities for co-regulation. The ability to soothe and be soothed, to talk and listen, to offer and receive, to fluidly move in and out of connection is centered in this newest part of the autonomic nervous system. Reciprocity, the mutual ebb and flow that defines nourishing relationships, is a function of the ventral vagus. As a result of its myelinated pathways, the ventral vagus provides rapid and organized responses. In a ventral vagal state, we have access to a range of responses including calm, happy, meditative, engaged, attentive, active, interested, excited, passionate, alert, ready, relaxed, savoring, and joyful.

This biological need for co-regulation with others is not dissimilar to the concept of limbic revision — “the power to remodel the emotional parts of the people we love,” and to have our own emotional pathways remodeled by the people who love us. This is only possible in safe relationships, and it is the vagus system that governs our sense of safety.

Central to polyvagal theory is the distinction between conscious perception and what Porges termed neuroception — the conditioned way the autonomic nervous system responds from within the body, without our awareness, to cues of safety and danger in the outside world. Because our vagal pathways are shaped by our earliest experiences of co-regulation in the infant-parent dyad, ruptures in that co-regulation — whether by abuse or neglect — condition the dorsal vagus to become dominant and make a neuroception of danger the default response, storying reality away from safety, nowhere more perilously than in intimate relationships. Dana writes:

Co-regulation is at the heart of positive relationships… If we miss opportunities to co-regulate in childhood, we feel that loss in our adult relationships. Trauma, either in experiences of commission (acts of harm) or omission (absence of care), makes co-regulation dangerous and interrupts the development of our co-regulatory skills. Out of necessity, the autonomic nervous system is shaped to independently regulate. Clients will often say that they needed connection but there was no one in their life who was safe, so after a while they stopped looking. Through a polyvagal perspective, we know that although they stopped explicitly looking and found ways to navigate on their own, their autonomic nervous system never stopped needing, and longing for, co-regulation.

Because we are physiologies first and psychologies second, but we are also storytelling and sensemaking creatures, our minds naturally create emotional narratives out of these unconscious vagal states — stories that, if we are not careful enough and conscious enough, may come to subsume reality. Dana observes:

The mind narrates what the nervous system knows. Story follows state.

Our early adaptive survival responses of trauma train the autonomic nervous system on a default neuroception of danger, replacing patterns of connection with patterns of protection in a fear-based narrative. And yet these reflexes can be recalibrated by retraining our regulatory pathways.

Because the feeling of reciprocity is one of the most powerful regulators of the autonomic nervous system, a great deal of repair and rewiring can happen in relationships winged with true reciprocity. Dana writes:

Reciprocity is a connection between people that is created in the back-and-forth communication between two autonomic nervous systems. It is the experience of heartfelt listening and responding. We are nourished in experiences of reciprocity, feeling the ebb and flow, giving and receiving, attunement, and resonance.

But the great paradox is that if our earliest template of connection is marked by rupture and deficient co-regulation, our very notion of reciprocity may be warped, leading us to tolerate immense asymmetries of affection and attention, to mistake deeply imbalanced relationships for reciprocal. The grounds for optimism lie in the very real possibility of changing the template through safe and nourishing relationships — ones we may not so much choose at first, for trauma can taint our choices with unhealthy patterns, as chance into and only then choose to nurture. The payoff is a gradual transition from the dorsal vagal state into the ventral vagal, a gradual willingness to release the patterns of protection in favor of connection, allowing the kinds of relationships Adrienne Rich celebrated as ones “in which two people have the right to use the word ‘love.'”

Complement with the science of how emotion are made and how love rewires the brain, then revisit Toni Morrison on reclaiming the body as an instrument of joy, sanity, and self-love.

#9291. A Forgotten Remedy for Depression

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Devon Frye

There’s growing concern about the risks of antidepressants, including side effects and withdrawal symptoms. Many people who are taking antidepressants are now turning to deprescribing resources, while others who are experiencing depression are wondering whether they should start taking antidepressants at all or if there’s another way.

But there’s one remedy that hasn’t gotten the attention it deserves: exercise.

In what follows, I’ll look at the surprising antidepressant effects of exercise, why it isn’t prescribed more widely, and a simple framework to help people get started.

One of the most astonishing findings in recent depression research is that exercise can be as effective as antidepressants, and some studies suggest it may be even more effective for mild to moderate depression. Millions of people have been prescribed powerful psychiatric drugs, often without being told that something as ordinary as walking, jogging, cycling, or strength training might provide comparable benefits.

The evidence has become increasingly difficult to ignore. Exercise ranks as one of the most effective known lifestyle interventions for depression. These include aerobic exercises, walking, jogging, strength training, and yoga. Intriguingly, evidence suggests that strength training is slightly more effective for women and younger adults, and yoga for men and older adults.

Exercise isn't just about shedding calories. It improves inflammation, metabolism, sleep, and the body's response to stress. These are precisely the factors that can go wrong in depression. But I think there's something deeper going on.

I've argued that depression may be a functional signal: our brain's way of telling us that something in our lives isn't going well and needs more attention. Sometimes the problem is a relationship, a job, or a life goal that no longer suits us. But sometimes the problem is the way we're living.

Humans evolved to move. Our ancestors spent much of their days walking, gathering food, carrying things, and engaging physically with the world. They didn't spend eight hours sitting in front of a computer, followed by another four hours staring at a smartphone. Yet that's how many of us live today.

Is it surprising that our bodies, and our minds, are protesting? Perhaps depression is telling us that something is wrong with the lives we've built for ourselves.

The evidence for the benefits of exercise is strong enough that a group of psychiatrists recently asked, in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, whether failing to prescribe exercise for depression could amount to “psychiatric malpractice.”

Part of the problem, they argue, is training. In one survey, 92 percent of mental health professionals said they'd received no formal training in prescribing exercise, and 41 percent said they never prescribe it at all.

Still, simply telling people to “be active” rarely works. People who struggle with depression need guidance and support.

For those for whom exercise is a real possibility, the same group offers a simple framework called FITT, which stands for frequency, intensity, time, and type. As a rule of thumb (and obviously to be adjusted for each person's physical health and other medical conditions):

But they also emphasize that less is better than none. Even one or two sessions a week, or 10 to 30 minutes at a time, can help.

Sometimes, what depression may be pointing to is precisely the mismatch between how we are designed to live and how we actually live. Exercise may be one way of answering its call.

#9290. Four Levels Of Customer Understanding

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Many companies think they know fairly well what their users want and need, and how they make their decisions. Yet most of the time these are merely big assumptions and big hunches — with little real evidence to support them. In practice, obvious reasons might be true, but they rarely paint the full picture.

To understand our customers, we must triangulate across four levels of customer understanding by Hannah Shamji. It’s a useful way to think about the underlying reasons for user behavior, hidden motivations, and the complex layers of messy and noisy reality that are often overlooked. Let’s see how it works.

To learn about customers, it might seem reasonable to ask people what they think and draw conclusions from it. But it’s rarely an effective way to get actionable answers. In fact, as it turns out, what people think, feel, say, and do are often very different things.

As Erika Hall wrote, asking a question directly is the worst way to get a true and useful answer to that question. We don’t always understand or are aware of our true motivations. We often apply our own context and interpretations to questions.

We also exaggerate (a lot!). We focus on edge cases and unrealistic scenarios, and we favor short-term goals over long-term goals. So if users say that they absolutely need to compare products in a table, it doesn’t mean that they couldn’t get to their underlying goal without it.

Just to indicate how tricky listening to words alone is: even little nuances in words chosen matter. In practice, users are rarely precise in expressing their thoughts, and a good example is the distinction between possible, plausible, and probable, as discovered by Thomas D’hooge.

A study on Dutch verbal probability terms shows how unreliable the choice of words is. While extreme words have some agreement, terms like “possible,” “maybe,” “uncertain,” or “likely” lead to a wide spread of interpretations. So we shouldn’t rely on what people say, but rather try to go deeper.

To get a more realistic and less biased view of customers’ needs, we need to understand a broader picture across 4 levels:

Personally, I wouldn’t recommend NPS (alternative). It’s worth noting that different levels might reveal conflicting or contradictory data. To get a better understanding, we need to triangulate and reconcile data with mixed-method research.

Emotions are always difficult to capture, but they are easier to spot once you observe people doing what they need to do without external influence or interruptions. The ability to positively impact users grows by moving from sympathy to empathy or even compassion, as articulated by Sarah Gibbons.

In the past, I was using “speak-aloud” protocol and asked users to walk me through their thought process as they were completing tasks. But it actually turns out to be quite disruptive. Because people are focused on speaking at the same time while solving a task, many emotions remain hidden or obscured by their language.

So, when conducting usability testing, I don’t ask users to speak through their experience. Instead, I observe where they tap or hover with the mouse, where their mouse circles without an action, where they scroll, and how long. Eventually, when a user confirms that they are done or that they are stuck, I ask questions.

The Emotion Wheel (website) by Geoffrey Roberts is a helpful little tool for better describing a range of emotions during user interviews or design sessions. It certainly needs refinement for product design needs, but it helps us get more precise about the sentiment customers or colleagues might be experiencing, moving beyond just “good” or “bad”.

One helpful trick is to use mirroring — repeating what a user has said, or ask the same question twice, just paraphrasing it. Or navigating the emotions wheel (see above) to better capture and understand the emotion.

These strategies help uncover some of the issues that perhaps didn’t come up in the first answer. That’s also when a user tends to add more useful context and details as they explain their confusion.

I think that Alin brings up a very strong argument, and personally, I find it difficult to disagree with. However, I do see user’s emotional response as a signal of how well the product is working for them. How engaged or detached they are in their journey, how they react to aesthetics, how confused or confident they are.

Ultimately, these are signals. To make a difference, we must go beyond emotions and explore what people actually do. Usually, this means relentlessly observing, diagnosing, and focusing on underlying user needs.

Instead of asking, we need to observe. Usually, I focus on small things that make or break an experience. I see where users lose time, repeat actions, hover without clicking, or click and then go back. Pay attention to subtle cues like scratching their neck, raising eyebrows, or expressions of worry, joy, or confusion.

Many companies talk about “validation” through user testing, but often that means simply confirming existing assumptions. But we should instead diagnose existing behavior without preconceived notions or affiliations. We don’t validate — we actually research instead.

That research means not just understanding customers’ real motivations, but also risks, doubts, concerns, worries, and perhaps even harms.

The only way to get there is by building a sincere, honest, and trustworthy relationship — one that feels right and resonates deeply. When customers truly care and want to help, getting to a real understanding becomes much, much easier.

We don’t need expensive tools to uncover user needs. David Travis provides a fantastic overview of helpful strategies to do just that. Here are some initiatives to spread the word about real user’s struggles or gain a deeper understanding of user needs:

The core idea here is that you don’t need extensive and expensive tools to uncover user needs. You need to create spaces where customers’ struggles can be exposed and make these struggles visible across the entire company.

It can be short video clips of user sessions or a monthly newsletter with what we learned this month. Making these pain points visible can rally everyone from marketing to engineering to keep users’ struggles at the back of their minds.

To make an impact, we must go way beyond user feedback. It’s never enough to listen to surveys — we must observe customers’ actual behaviors and build relationships to truly understand their goals and their motivations.

And most importantly, we need to understand what questions we actually want to have answered. Not what “validation” we need to move on with the project, but what we don’t know and what we need to research.

Without it, everything else is merely hunches and assumptions — and often wrong and expensive ones.

#9289. New book charts American artist’s lifelong devotion to the South Seas

Robert Lee Eskridge’s Stone-Fishing (around 1930) shows the Polynesian fishing practice of using ropes and stones Courtesy of www.GalleryHawaiiana.com

This is a book about a love affair, one that ran so deep it yielded thousands of watercolours, hundreds of oil paintings and three illustrated books. The painter Robert Lee Eskridge (1891-1975) first visited the South Seas in May 1927, when his ship pulled into the harbour of Papeete, Tahiti. Seeking respite from the grey skies and bone-chilling winters of Chicago, he was instantly smitten and kept returning to the South Seas, eventually making his home in Honolulu, Hawai’i.

Little in Eskridge’s early life had predicted that infatuation. Born in Philadelphia, he attended the Art Institute of Chicago, studied in Paris with the Cubist painter André Lhote, and travelled across Europe for three years. His style, fusing Art Deco patterns with a form of relaxed realism, won him gigs as an illustrator and artist, culminating in a high-profile commission to produce murals for the lobby of the newly rebuilt Palmer House hotel in Chicago. On the eve of his departure for Tahiti, he chose Marco Polo as his subject. (The murals were painted over in 1966.)

Falling in love with the South Seas is not a unique experience. Names like Herman Melville, Robert Louis Stevenson and Paul Gauguin conjure lush tropical forests, foam-crested waves lapping pristine beaches, and carefree Islanders performing hula dances: a vision inevitably darkened by the damages wrought by colonialism. The Islanders Eskridge painted, unlike Gauguin’s, are not immobilised by the artist’s desire to project meaning into them. They are walking, working, dancing, fishing and making music, living fully in the present even as they honour their rich traditions.

Eskridge’s enthusiasm for Islander culture finds a perfect match in biographer Cook’s enthusiasm for Eskridge. While the more lyrically effusive passages in this volume might not appeal to everyone, the lavish illustrations drawn from multiple collections and the excellent captions help us understand the breadth, range and sophistication of a supremely adaptable painter who deserves to be better known. (Regrettably, some images—of the lost Chicago murals, for example—are AI-produced).

Eskridge’s paintings, whether they show bustling street scenes or re-create rituals he witnessed, vibrate with life. As a young man, he was entranced with Sandro Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (around 1485, in the Uffizi Gallery), and that painting’s revelatory spirit lingers on in Eskridge’s bright, luminous colours or in the way he arranges groups of people around a central figure or an activity.

His training under Lhote shapes the cascading abstract forms Eskridge uses in the background of works such as Stone Fishing (around 1930, Gallery Hawaiiana). In this ancient Polynesian fishing practice, men use ropes with stones to herd leaping fish into shallower waters—a communal effort as well as an occasion for individual daring, represented here beautifully by the young man in the middle, who jumps to grab a fish from the air. A later masterpiece is Hilo Wharf (around 1949, Honolulu Museum of Art), a harbour scene, in which Eskridge blends shirtless workers and the bodies of gigantic tuna fish, some already packed up, into an intense drama of shapes, colour and movement.

Since Eskridge treated the Islanders and their culture with respect, they accepted him as one of their own, Cook tells us. They even asked Eskridge to represent them at the Chicago World’s Fair in 1933. Invitations followed to provide Hawaiian-themed murals for the McCoy Pavilion in Honolulu’s Ala Moana Park and, later, to design clothes for the Hawai’ian label Paradise Sportswear.

Always one to defy expectations, Eskridge, at age 64, married Helen Gebhardt and settled in Olympia, Washington. But the Islands kept calling. He died in April 1975 at a hotel in Honolulu named, appropriately, Hale-kulani, “house befitting heaven”.

• C.J. Cook, Robert Lee Eskridge, South Pacific Dreams Publishing, 344pp, 509 col. illust., $59.95 (hb), published 11 August

• Christoph Irmscher is a critic and biographer

#9288. I Feel, Therefore I Am: Neuroscientist Antonio Damasio the Consciousness of the Body

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood.
